articles.title: Steve Tandy: Wales boss on tough Nations Championship calls in World Cup countdown
articles.summary: Wales boss Steve Tandy on making tough Nations Championship selection calls as he counts down to the 2027 World Cup in Australia.
articles.body:
After over a year and 13 games as Wales head coach, Steve Tandy is getting used to making tough phone calls and then copping flak when his selections are made public.

Tandy named his 39-man squad for November's Nations Championship on Tuesday, with the 11am announcement prompting the usual tribal responses.

There was delight at the inclusions of uncapped trio Aneurin Owen, Che Hope and Rhys Barratt and recalls for Rio Dyer, Seb Davies, Taine Basham and Gabriel Hamer-Webb.

There was also disappointment at the omissions of Taulupe Faletau, Macs Page, Elliot Dee, Bryn Bradley, Mason Grady and Tommy Reffell, who Tandy later revealed had suffered a knee injury.

"There'll be people out there challenging me on selections," said the head coach, who has now named four squads.

"No-one really says who they would leave out either, it's always the people that should be in! It's something that comes with the territory."

Wales great Faletau still has drive for fourth World Cup

Uncapped Dragons get Wales Nations Championship call

Tandy left his role as Scotland's defence coach to call the shots for his country in the summer of 2025.

He has used 54 players so far and is still casting his net wide despite it being just under a year until the World Cup gets under way.

Tandy will be limited to 33 players for the tournament in Australia but has selected a squad of 39 for the Nations Championship.

"I cop flak wherever I go, that's something I'm getting used to. I get some of that, but you can only pick so many," said the former Ospreys flanker and boss.

"Martyn [Williams, team manager] would have kicked off if I had gone with more, he wouldn't be happy with the budget!

"I'm comfortable in this space and know that we are thorough around our selection.

"There have been some brilliant performances out there from boys that are not in. I've had some phone calls over the last few days that were tough, but I'd rather the boys know where they sit."

Wales counting down the year until World Cup

Will Wales tackle reliance on Williams before World Cup?

Opportunity knocks in World Cup countdown

Wales have just 12 or 13 games until they get their World Cup campaign under way against Zimbabwe.

It would be understandable if Tandy was keen to whittle down his options, but he is still keen to reward performances.

"I'd never give out an opportunity, they've got to earn it, and I think I am pretty clear on the core of our group," he said.

"But this is another opportunity to see someone else in our environment and see what comes out of it."

That is the case with the uncapped Dragons pair of centre Owen and scrum-half Hope, but the selection of their Rodney Parade team-mate Davies was more surprising.

The lock or flanker, in his second season with Dragons after moving from Cardiff, has 17 caps, but has not featured since facing Italy in the 2022 Six Nations.

Wales already have Dafydd Jenkins, Ben Carter, Adam Beard and Teddy Williams in their squad and are highly unlikely to take five second-row forwards to the World Cup, but Tandy is still keen to cast his eye over the 30-year-old.

"You see the athletic ability with Seb and speaking to him there was the emotional outpouring of being involved with the squad," Tandy said.

"We had an alignment camp – a smaller unit gathering – and he came in to get to know them. With that exposure, it's a great opportunity to see boys in our environment."

One in-form player who must wait for his opportunity is Page, who has caught the eye on the wing for Scarlets.

The 21-year-old has scored four tries in four appearances, while he has made nine line breaks.

He misses out with Dyer and Hamer-Webb coming in to join Josh Adams, Ellis Mee, Blair Murray, Tom Rogers and Louis Rees-Zammit.

"Macs has been outstanding but that's where the depth of our wingers and back field is really encouraging," Tandy told Scrum V podcast.

"Look at others - Mason Grady, Keelan Giles, Tom Bowen, all those boys are playing well. Jacob Beetham was outstanding at the start of the season [before injury]."

Dyer was selected by Tandy last autumn and won his 24th cap against South Africa, but missed out on the Six Nations and summer Tests.

The Dragons back has been a threat with ball in hand and, like Scarlets rival Mee, has thrived when chasing restarts and kicks.

"Some of his aerial contests have been better than anyone in Wales," said Tandy.

"Rio has really developed that and his work rate has been outstanding. He thoroughly deserves his recall."

Tandy has fielded five different midfield partnerships so far, and could add to that tally after Owen's call-up.

Ben Thomas started against South Africa in July but misses out because of a calf injury, with the uncapped Dragons centre now pushing for a chance at 12.

Owen, a member of the Wales squad in the summer 2021 after a breakthrough season when he broke up the expected partnership of Jamie Roberts and Nick Tompkins, has been rewarded for club excellence.

"He has been outstandingly consistent and does everything really well. Speak to coaches and they mention his standards on and off the field, how he is the last one off after working on extras," Tandy told Scrum V .

"He has had injuries, and you could argue he could have been in the selection mix sooner, but what I love is that he has kept going and kept getting better.

"He has been so consistent and at a high level, not just seven out of 10 but above that."

Owen is a specialist 12 to rival Joe Hawkins, who is with Scarlets in South Africa to play Stormers this weekend along with Taine Plumtree.

Eddie James is one of the five Wales squad members to stay at home, with Tandy likely to field him in the Nations Championship opener against Japan.

There has been debate about the powerful back's best position - with many feeling he has the bulk for inside centre, where he started Scarlets' first two games of the season - but Tandy is sticking to his guns.

"I see Eddie more as a 13. He can definitely play 12, as we have seen for the Scarlets, but in our team he is more of a 13 who can play 12," he said.

"Louie Hennessey, Max Llewellyn and Eddie, they have big frames and there is lot of interchangeability for the 12s and 13s. We have a nice variety of options there."

Tandy has made his first selection of the Nations Championship, but there is plenty more scrutiny ahead with four team announcements to come.

articles.title: Ireland rugby: Key questions as head coach Andy Farrell prepares to name Nations Championship squad
articles.summary: A look at some of the key questions facing Ireland head coach Andy Farrell as he prepares to name his Nations Championship squad on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell's latest squad selection this week is likely to stir debate about how his team are shaping up with less than a year to go until the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

On Wednesday, Farrell will reveal his panel for next month's Nations Championship home leg, which includes home matches against Argentina, Fiji and back-to-back world champions South Africa before the finals weekend at Twickenham.

Ireland opened their Nations Championship campaign with wins over Australia and Japan before a 40-21 loss to New Zealand in Auckland.

After November, the Six Nations will be Farrell's only extended period of competitive action with his squad before they travel to Australia for the showpiece tournament.

As ever, Farrell has plenty to consider, with the usual injury concerns and several players pushing for inclusion with strong displays during the opening weeks of the season.

Last weekend was particularly pleasing for Farrell, as Leinster, Munster, Connacht and Ulster all began their European campaigns with victories .

Before Wednesday's squad announcement, BBC Sport examines some of the key questions facing the Ireland boss.

The Ireland squad will be announced at 15:00 BST on Wednesday.

Ireland v Argentina, 6 November, Aviva Stadium, 20:10

Ireland v Fiji, 14 November, Aviva Stadium, 20:10

Ireland v South Africa, 21 November, Aviva Stadium, 16:40

Nations Championship finals weekend fixture (opponent TBD), 27-29 November, Allianz Stadium Twickenham

Farrell will be without some key men in November.

Having missed the July games with Australia, Japan and New Zealand, captain Caelan Doris is still unavailable as he recovers from knee and foot issues.

With Doris already sidelined, Farrell would have been concerned to see Jack Conan leaving Stade Marcel-Michelin with his arm in a sling after the province's Champions Cup win over Clermont on Saturday.

The potential absence of both Doris and Conan could create an opportunity for Sean Jansen, who scored a try on his Test debut against Japan before featuring off the bench in the All Blacks defeat.

Fly-half Jack Crowley remains unavailable because of a vascular injury , and while first-choice scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park is expected to be included, the 34-year-old has not yet featured for Leinster this season because of a groin strain.

Props Jack Boyle and Paddy McCarthy are still missing, but Farrell can call upon first-choice loose-head Andrew Porter for the first time since last year's defeat by the Springboks in Dublin.

Porter, 30, missed the 2026 Six Nations with a calf problem and, having returned for Leinster in late March, he was ruled out of the July Tests with a similar issue.

Porter's Leinster team-mate Ryan Baird is also available again. The 27-year-old utility forward impressed at blind-side flanker during the 2025 autumn Tests before a fractured tibia forced him to miss the Six Nations. He returned for Leinster late last season but missed the July games.

Popular winger Mack Hansen is also back after an injury-ravaged 2025-26 season comprised of two Test appearances and a single run-out for Connacht.

With Crowley out, Sam Prendergast and Ciaran Frawley will battle for the number 10 jersey in November - and both players have caught the eye in recent weeks.

Prendergast has 17 caps for Ireland but has not had the smoothest introduction to Test rugby. A gifted operator with ball in hand, the 23-year-old's defensive frailties have been targeted by teams in the past and he was dropped by Farrell after a poor start to this year's Six Nations.

However, the Kildare-born out-half has sparkled for Leinster this season, picking up back-to-back man of the match awards in URC and Champions Cup wins over Cardiff and Clermont following displays that have showcased his sharpened running game.

While Prendergast has launched into this season impressively, the opening act of Frawley's Connacht career has been impossible to ignore.

Having moved out west from Leinster to secure regular gametime at 10, the 28-year-old has flourished for Stuart Lancaster's side, scoring four tries and starring in last week's thrilling 45-36 Champions Cup win over Saracens.

Ireland's win over Japan in July was Frawley's first Test start at 10. It would not be surprising to see one or two more next month.

Charlie O'Shea has impressed for Munster in recent weeks but Farrell may feel it is too soon to introduce the 20-year-old to Test rugby, while Joey Carbery could earn a recall despite making only one brief appearance off the bench since rejoining Leinster.

As mentioned above, Jansen is primed to play a key role in the back row, while uncapped Munster number eight Brian Gleeson could be included after impressing again in last week's win over Racing 92 .

Gleeson missed out on a possible Test debut 12 months ago when he was forced to withdraw from the squad with an elbow injury.

Garry Ringrose, Robbie Henshaw, Stuart McCloskey and Bundle Aki will likely make it as centre options, but Jamie Osborne may merit a run-out at 12 having recently featured there in Leinster's win over Cardiff.

In the front row, former England prop Kieran Brookes is pushing for inclusion.

The 36-year-old, an Ireland underage international before earning 16 caps for England, has showcased his solidity in the scrum since joining Munster in the summer.

Can Ireland claim statement Springboks win?

Having lost to the All Blacks in July, beating world champions South Africa less than a year out from the next tournament in Australia would be a major statement.

Ireland have won four of their past six meetings with the Springboks but last year's 24-13 reverse in Dublin, before 22 and 19-point losses to France and New Zealand respectively earlier this year were the latest humbling dust-ups with rugby's elite.

Last year's loss to South Africa was a particularly bruising night for Ireland as they picked up five cards and failed to match the might of the Springbok scrum.

While Farrell later praised his side's response to a chaotic first half which they ended with 12 men, claiming South Africa's scalp would be a major declaration of intent heading into a World Cup year.

South Africa have played six Tests since Ireland's last match against New Zealand. The Boks beat Argentina before securing a 3-1 Test series win over the All Blacks.

They did, however, fall to a 42-38 loss to Australia in Perth on 27 September.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: England suffer huge blow as Strange ruled out
articles.summary: Jasmin Strange's withdrawal from the England squad with a knee injury is a "devastating blow" to their World Cup prospects says head coach Stuart Barrow.
articles.body:
Jasmin Strange's withdrawal from the England squad with a knee injury is a "devastating blow" to their World Cup prospects says head coach Stuart Barrow.

The Sydney Roosters second-row forward impressed on her debut, scoring a try as England thrashed Wales 70-6 in their World Cup opener.

Strange, 23, whose mother was born in Yorkshire, was one of five NRLW players included in Barrow's squad to face the reigning world champions Australia in Perth.

"Jasmin joined us when we arrived here and has been outstanding. She's mixed with the girls really well and to lose her yesterday in training was a devastating blow for all the girls," said Barrow.

"It was almost a freak accident. It was a defensive session but Jasmin was with the ball, did a step and unfortunately suffered a serious knee injury. It was a real disappointing outcome for someone who has been excellent for us.

"It's affected the camp but Jasmin will want us to recover and bounce back and she's coming back into camp this evening so the girls will get around her.

"It flatlined the group and it flatlined the coaching staff but we've bounced back today. Within seven hours Jas had a scan and got the results. I went to the hospital with her last night and the scan confirmed our worst fears."

Strange, 23, who comes from a rugby league family, had looked set to be a key player for Barrow's new-look side which has altered significantly since England fell to a record defeat 90-4 defeat to the Jillaroos in March 2025.

Barrow confirmed that Leeds Rhinos second-row Lucy Murray will replace Strange this weekend and that there are no plans to bring in another player for the remainder of the tournament.

"She [Jasmin] played very well at the weekend so we lose a bit of quality but we've brought 23 players who are all competing for shirts so we are confident we can cover that loss," Barrow added.

"It'll be a straight swap. Lucy [Murray] was very close in the first selection and was close again this week so with Jas playing that back-row spot, Lucy will come straight in."

articles.title: Maro Itoje: Saracens in talks with England captain as Top 14 clubs circle
articles.summary: Saracens hope to extend Maro Itoje's deal amid reported interest from Top 14 clubs, which could spell the end of the England captain's Test career.
articles.body:
Saracens are hopeful of extending Maro Itoje's deal amid reported interest from Top 14 clubs, which could spell the end of the England captain's Test career.

Discussions are under way to extend Itoje's Saracens stay beyond its current expiry after next year's Rugby World Cup.

However, the second row will be 33 by the end of the tournament and faces potentially his final chance to take up longstanding interest in him from across the Channel.

Any move to France would put Itoje's Test career on hold, with the Rugby Football Union having a policy of not selecting overseas-based players.

While Saracens are optimistic of reaching a new agreement with Itoje, they are aware they are competing with Top 14 clubs with more spending power.

The headline salary cap in the French top flight stands at 11m euros (£9.2m), which is significantly higher than the Prem's equivalent figure of £6.4m.

The Top 14 also benefits from a more lucrative broadcast deal than its English equivalent, with a blockbuster five-year agreement with Canal Plus coming into effect from next season , external .

However, unlike in France, the English top flight allows one player at each club to sit outside the salary cap, in a so-called marquee spot, which may give Saracens more freedom to compete with overseas offers.

By staying in England, Itoje would also be eligible for a central England contract, worth about £150,000 a year.

As part of an agreement between clubs and country, Itoje was rested for England's summer fixtures against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina after several seasons of heavy workload.

While a move to the Top 14 would remove international fixtures from Itoje's schedule, French top-flight rugby is arduous.

As well as each club having 26 regular-season fixtures, the top six also qualify for the Top 14's post-season play-offs, with European fixtures on top.

Itoje has been at Saracens since he was a teenager, staying during their single season in the second-tier Championship after their punishment for repeated breaches of the salary cap.

Paris-based Racing 92 have been credited with an interest in Itoje in the past, without a move transpiring.

England's policy of only picking players from domestic rugby – a key protection for the domestic game - has come under pressure recently.

Jack Willis, who represented England at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, has enjoyed a stellar stint at Toulouse, winning the Top 14's player of the season award in each of the past two campaigns.

Former England captain Courtney Lawes, who has returned to the Prem and Sale after two seasons with Brive, has said he believes the bar should be scrapped . Ellis Genge, part of England's current leadership group, has also advocated a change , external .

The end of a Rugby World Cup cycle can be a convenient time for players to make a move abroad.

Willis was joined by fellow England internationals Joe Marchant and David Ribbans in the Top 14 immediately after the 2023 tournament while Lawes, Lewis Ludlam, Kyle Sinckler, Owen Farrell, Manu Tuilagi, Jonny May and Billy Vunipola made moves to France in the following summer.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Ireland without injured trio Jack Conan, Caelan Doris, Jack Crowley but Jamison Gibson-Park included
articles.summary: Jack Conan, Caelan Doris and Jack Crowley will miss Ireland’s Nations Championship Tests against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa next month due to injury; Jamison Gibson-Park has been included despite his recent groin problem, while Mack Hansen and Andrew Porter return to the squad
articles.body:
Ireland face Tests against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa next month without captain Caelan Doris and fly-half Jack Crowley, who are both expected to return from long-term injuries in January.

Doris has been sidelined by foot and knee problems, while Crowley is recovering from a vascular issue in his leg. Conan, who like Doris plays at No 8, is also ruled out after injuring his shoulder while playing for Leinster in the Champions Cup last weekend.

Scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park has yet to feature this season due to a groin injury but has been included in the 36-man squad. Mack Hansen, Andrew Porter and Ryan Baird also return to the squad after recovering from injury.

Two uncapped players have made the squad in Ulster fly-half Jamie Benson and back-row James McNabney, while Dan Sheehan has been named as captain.

The IRFU also list Jack Boyle, Harry Byrne, Iain Henderson, Paddy McCarthy, Calvin Nash and Bryn Ward as out through injury.

Omissions include Munster quartet Jeremy Loughman, Edwin Edogbo, Thomas Ahern and Brian Gleeson, Connacht's Finlay Bealham, as well as Ulster's Cormac Izuchukwu.

articles.title: Canada v England: Ellie Kildunne on bench as Red Roses ring changes
articles.summary: Star full-back Ellie Kildunne is dropped to the bench as England shake up selection in response to a first defeat in four years.
articles.body:
Star full-back Ellie Kildunne has been dropped to the bench as England shake up their selection in response to a first defeat in four years.

Kildunne was part of the starting XV who lost 24-21 to Canada last Friday in Toronto with the Red Roses' unbeaten streak ending at 41 matches.

Head coach John Mitchell has accused his side of losing the hunger that fuelled a run which took in four successive Six Nations Grand Slams and last year's landmark world title on home soil.

"Last Friday, we lost sight of what we could control when it mattered most. That's on us to fix," said Mitchell.

"This week is about getting back to who we are - hungry, accountable to each other and demanding more of ourselves than anyone outside this group ever could."

Emma Sing comes in at full-back in Kildunne's place for Saturday's rematch (00:00 BST) against Canada in Ottawa, while Tatyana Heard and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald - backline starters in the defeat - drop out of the matchday squad entirely.

Helena Rowland and Mia Venner replace Heard and Moloney-MacDonald at inside centre and wing respectively.

In the fourth change to the starting line-up, Sadia Kabeya, who appeared off the bench last week on her comeback from a leg injury, starts with Alex Matthews, two-time Rugby World Cup winner, dropping to the bench.

Exeter's Flo Robinson and Sale's Hollie Aitchison are included on the bench as a new-look set of half-back replacements.

Sing, a rangy runner who can also kick goals, started two matches at full-back during England's Six Nations campaign, with Kildunne switching to a different position on the wing on each occasion.

Sing's Gloucester-Hartpury team-mate Venner made her England debut in 2020 aged just 17.

Venner has won only another four caps since but was putting pressure on England's more established back three at the start of this year, appearing in wins over Scotland and Italy.

The 24-year-old finished as the PWR's joint top try-scorer last season, crossing 12 times.

Moloney-MacDonald cost her side an early try in the defeat by Canada when, after doing superbly to pick Jess Breach's pass off her toes, she spilled the ball over the line in the sixth minute.

"We've earned a strong period but nothing about it is owed to us going forward," said Mitchell.

"Friday [Saturday 00:00 BST] is an opportunity to apply sustained pressure, learn from what we missed and come out the other side better than we went in."

Head coach John Mitchell has made four changes to the starting XV in total, with Gloucester-Hartpury duo Emma Sing and Mia Venner coming into the back three at full-back and wing respectively, while Helena Rowland of Loughborough Lightning returns at inside-centre.

In the forwards, there is just one amendment to the team that began the second Test - Sadia Kabeya, also of Loughborough Lightning, is selected at openside flanker.

While Kildunne - 2024's World Player of the Year - and back-row Alex Matthews move to the replacements bench, wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and centre Tatyana Heard drop out of the squad altogether.

"Friday is our first chance to respond," Mitchell said.

"Last Friday, we lost sight of what we could control when it mattered most; that's on us to fix. This week is about getting back to who we are: hungry, accountable to each other and demanding more of ourselves than anyone outside this group ever could.

articles.title: Ireland Rugby: Jamie Benson and James McNabney handed first call-ups
articles.summary: Ulster duo Jamie Benson and James McNabney have been handed their first Ireland call-ups for November's Nations Championship matches.
articles.body:
Ulster duo Jamie Benson and James McNabney have been handed their first Ireland call-ups for November's Nations Championship matches.

Former England Under-20 international Benson joined Ulster from Harlequins in the off-season and is Irish qualified through his Belfast-born mother.

The 24-year-old has featured at centre for the majority of his short Ulster career to date but can also play at fly-half.

Back row McNabney, 23, had been in Ireland training squads before and returned to action over the summer after a year on the sidelines with an ACL injury.

Prop Andrew Porter, forward Ryan Baird and wings Mack Hansen and Tommy O'Brien all return to the squad after missing the summer's matches.

Head coach Andy Farrell has a had to deal with a lengthy injury list, with captain Caelan Doris among those sidelined.

Fly-half Jack Crowley is also missing through injury, as is Jack Boyle, Harry Byrne, Jack Conan, Iain Henderson, Paddy McCarthy, Calvin Nash and Bryn Ward.

In the absence of Doris, his Leinster team-mate Dan Sheehan will captain Ireland.

Scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park has been named despite not featuring for Leinster this season with a groin injury.

"It's always going to test you when you've got a couple of injuries in one position," Farrell said.

"But that's not just up to the guys who are stepping in, it's also up to the rest of the squad to make sure that we're all rolling together and keep taking steps forward."

The Ulster duo of Zac Ward and Cormac Izuchukwu have missed out on selection, as has Munster prop Jeremy Loughman.

Ireland will face Argentina at the Aviva Stadium on Friday, 6 November before Fiji travel to Dublin on 14 November.

Farrell's side then host world champions South Africa on 21 November before the finals weekend at the Allianz Stadium in London the following week.

Ireland started their Nations Championship campaign with victories over Australia and Japan but New Zealand came out on top in the third summer Test.

Farrell said it was "always great" to give players their first international call-ups, and both Benson and McNabney were players had he followed for some time.

Before he had even played a match for Ulster, Benson had been training with Ireland over the summer, while McNabney, who Farrell described as "some specimen of a man", also has training camp experience.

"It was great to get to know him and see what he's all about," Farrell said on Benson.

"He started the season really well and in a few different positions for Ulster, and that shows his versatility."

With the World Cup now less than one year away, Farrell added he wants his side to "keep progressing" over the next 12 months.

Ireland have had a mixed 2026 as they won the Triple Crown but missed out on the Six Nations title to France.

They narrowly beat the Wallabies in their Nations Championship opener and while they had to much for Japan, New Zealand were too strong in the third game of the tour of the southern hemisphere.

Argentina will be a tough start to the autumn matches, before Fiji and especially South Africa will provide more stern opposition.

"It's always great to get back in front of your home supporters and we know that's going to be needed," Farrell said.

"The box office games, those are the type of games that we want to play in. We want to keep on testing ourselves."

articles.title: Hyron Andrews: Former Sale second row died of natural causes - autopsy
articles.summary: Former Sale player Hyron Andrews - who was found dead at his new team's hotel base before a Champions Cup match - died of natural causes, an autopsy finds.
articles.body:
Hyron Andrews - the former Sale second row found dead at his new team's hotel base before a Champions Cup match in France on Saturday - died of natural causes, an autopsy has found.

The 31-year-old, who joined the Johannesburg-based Lions this summer, suffered a tear in the aorta, an artery which carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body.

The rupture led to blood filling the muscle sac surrounding his heart.

Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle, with investigators working on the theory that he had either suffered a fall, a heart attack or, as transpired, an aneurysm, where a bulging blood vessel breaks.

A tear in the aorta is a rare and dangerous medical condition, which can be caused by undetected high blood pressure or a birth defect.

His body is yet to be returned to his native South Africa.

Andrews' wife Maighlin, with whom he had two young sons, has asked for "respect, privacy and patience during this difficult time as the repatriation process begins", according to a statement from the Lions. , external

His team-mates went ahead with their game against La Rochelle on Saturday in his honour.

The visitors were applauded into the Stade Marcel-Deflandre by home fans, , external while several of the Lions players were in tears during a minute's silence before kick-off.

Sale, with whom Andrews spent two and half seasons, also paid tribute, with director of rugby Alex Sanderson saying that his team "to a man, loved playing with Hyron and being around him".

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: England 'not thinking about points difference' before France game, says Brad O'Neill
articles.summary: England suffered Rugby League World Cup opening game loss to Tonga; they now have to get a large win against France and then beat Papua New Guinea handsomely to keep slim hopes of progressing to the semi-finals alive; England play France on Saturday October 24 at 7.35am
articles.body:
An opening 30-12 defeat to Tonga has left their hopes of reaching the semi-finals hanging by a thread, with points difference looking increasingly like the only way to progress.

But head coach Brian McDermott has named an unchanged 19-man matchday squad, a sign that he does not plan radical changes against a France team smarting from their 78-4 humbling by Samoa.

O'Neill, the newly-crowned Super League Man of Steel, said: "We have discussed what is required but I feel like the mentality can't be any different to what we had against Tonga.

"We can't go into this game thinking about the points difference. We've got to go into this game hard-nosed like we did against Tonga, and hopefully if we do our jobs well enough we're going to get the win."

A complicated cross-group format has left England needing Tonga to beat Samoa in their final group game in a fortnight's time to stand any chance of reaching the last four - provided all the other games go to form.

That would take the final semi-final slot down to points difference between England and Samoa - and McDermott's men are already up against it given Samoa's stunning win over the Super League-laden French side.

"I feel like we play France in Super League most weeks with Catalans and Toulouse, so there will be some familiar faces," O'Neill added.

"We're expecting a great game at the weekend. France are coming off a loss, like us as well, so they are going to come out firing.

"But we're not changing anything about the way we play. It's more about working on the execution side of things that we didn't do so well against Tonga. As you'd expect, Saturday was very disappointing, but there is still a real belief in this team."

England must regroup ahead of facing France in Perth next Saturday, kick-off 7.35am (UK and Ireland time). Meanwhile, England women face Australia at 10.05am.

articles.title: Hyron Andrews: South African rugby player died of natural causes, team statement says
articles.summary: Hyron Andrews died suddenly in France at the age of 31; Andrews previously played for English club Sale Sharks; A club statement from South African rugby side Lions said he died from natural causes associated with his heart
articles.body:
The statement, citing French authorities who conducted the autopsy, said Andrews' death last week at the age of 31 ahead of a game in France was found to be caused by "a tear in the aorta (due to natural causes)".

The aorta is the main artery leading away from the heart.

"The Andrews family asks for respect, privacy and patience during this difficult time as the repatriation process begins," the statement added.

"A timeline for the return of Hyron's body to South Africa has not yet been determined."

Andrews played as a lock for the Johannesburg-based Lions and was found dead at the team's hotel in France last week ahead of a Champions Cup against La Rochelle, a French prosecutor told The Associated Press at the time.

A statement at the time of his death from SA rugby said that Andrews "passed away tragically, following an accident" and that he had "died after falling" at the team hotel.

Andrews' jersey was placed on the field as tribute was paid to him ahead of the game, with several Lions players in tears.

The 31-year-old South African second-row forward had spent the previous two years of his career playing for Sale Sharks in England before returning home this summer to join the Lions.

articles.title: Ciaran Frawley: Could Connacht fly-half earn Ireland starting spot?
articles.summary: After an impressive start to life at Connacht, former Ireland scrum-half Conor Murray feels Ciaran Frawley is a player to watch this autumn.
articles.body:
Since the retirement of Johnny Sexton in 2023, the topic of who should be Ireland's first-choice fly-half has been a never-ending discussion.

Sam Prendergast looked to have taken charge earlier this year but, after a shaky start to the Six Nations, Jack Crowley was handed the keys and impressed for the rest of the tournament.

When Crowley picked up a back injury at the end of last season, Prendergast slotted back in the 10 jersey for the summer's Nations Championship matches against Australia and New Zealand.

Ciaran Frawley got his chance against Japan and put in a solid display but, with Crowley and Harry Byrne injured, can he now establish himself as first choice under Andy Farrell?

For former Ireland scrum-half Conor Murray, he is one to watch.

Murray said Prendergast played "really well" as he was named player of the match in Leinster's Investec Champions Cup win over Clermont on Saturday, but Frawley has also caught his eye.

Fresh from a summer move which has taken him out of the shadows at Leinster, where he was rarely deployed at fly-half, to first choice at Connacht, the 28-year-old has settled in seamlessly under Stuart Lancaster.

Benson and McNabney handed first Ireland call-ups

In Dublin, he was often down the pecking order at fly-half, and often featured at full-back or at centre, and it felt like his versatility counted against him.

After moving west, Frawley scored twice on his debut against Benetton in the United Rugby Championship, and grabbed another two tries in Saturday's thrilling Champions Cup win over Saracens in Galway.

"It is one to watch in terms of seeing how much say he'll have [in November]," Murray told BBC Sport NI.

"I suspect that Sam is going in as number one choice, but Frawley is one to keep an eye on."

Murray said the quality of Ireland's goal kicking was still "the elephant in the room", and pointed to that fact that Frawley has not been kicking from the tee for Connacht.

While it was against lower-ranked opposition than Ireland will face in November - with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa all to visit Dublin - Frawley did land three of his four attempts for Ireland in the victory over Japan in July.

He also delivered in clutch moments, when his last-gasp drop goal in South Africa in 2024 secured a second-ever Test win in Springbok territory and a series draw with the world champions.

Aside from a number of injuries to signifcant players - such as captain Caelan Doris - Farrell named a settled squad for November's three Nations Championship matches.

Argentina come to the Aviva Stadium on 7 November, before matches against Fiji and South Africa and the inaugural finals weekend in London.

The Ulster duo of Jamie Benson and James McNabney, who Farrell described as a "specimen", are the only two new faces for the autumn fixtures.

Murray added that the squad was "as expected" from Farrell, and he believes the new Nations Championship can help preparations for the World Cup in Australia next year.

"You're obviously aware there's a World Cup and you want to be on that squad," said Murray, who won two Six Nations Grand Slams in a decorated career.

"They might use it as a building block and form it as a mini-tournament leading up to the World Cup, or try to replicate scenarios with the way the games are going to go, to lead up to a final.

"Does he treat the games as a last-16, a quarter-final, a semi-final and a final? It's important."

articles.title: Phil Vickery: England Rugby World Cup winner shares bodybuilding journey
articles.summary: Why England Rugby World Cup winner Phil Vickery has started entering bodybuilding competitions at the age of 50.
articles.body:
It could have been deep in the bowels of English rugby's national stadium in Twickenham.

Instead, Phil Vickery was backstage at the Physical Culture Show in Hull, waiting for his moment - but this time as a bodybuilder.

"It reminded me of being in the changing room before the big game, your nerves - are you going to be sick, you're happy, you're not happy, I can do this, this is raw," he said, adding that just recalling that moment earlier this month makes his hair stand on end.

"That nervous energy and waiting and then, oh, it's just a horrific feeling. All the girls and boys can relate to that, because that's the same at whatever level of sport you play.

"I'm questioning myself, should I even be there? But then you go, actually, do you know what? I've done the work. I've done the graft."

What started as an ambition to get fit has ignited a passion for mental and physical fitness, and for Vickery being the best version of himself.

Then came a challenge from his friend Lee Powell and, with support from his physical trainer Dave Campbell, Vickery entering bodybuilding competitions at the age of 50. Posing to the strains of the familiar World Cup anthem World in Union.

"What it probably did for me is ignite that ex-pro rugby player in me of detail, discipline, turning up when it's dark and dingy and cold, competing, and we went from there," Vickery said.

"What I've fallen in love with, with the bodybuilding, it's a very singular, isolated sport, because it is you against you. It's not about anyone else.

"There is no out. You can't hide behind a keyboard. You are stood on stage. Your physique and what you look like is a direct reflection of your effort and what you have done, and that is quite scary."

The former Gloucester and Wasps prop won 73 caps for England, five more for the British and Irish Lions.

Victory at the 2003 Rugby World Cup in Australia was a sporting zenith in a career that includes being a businessman and a Celebrity MasterChef winner.

But personal struggles and a diagnosis for probable CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy), for which Vickery is part of a continuing litigation battle, means he has had to manage his mental health.

"We all deal with things differently," he said. "I think having the gym and having that space to be able to work is really important for my mental health, but also for my body physically, because it is broken, so I use it in that sense.

"I think the one thing I really struggled with when I finished playing is I trained to play and I couldn't find that reason to train afterwards.

"And although you should train for yourself or your wellbeing, it probably took a low point or something to actually trigger it.

"But, probably, the bodybuilding - or doing the show or doing the original transformation - I have to close the circle. You know, you have a plan, you make a plan, you implement it, you commit to it, see it through, and then it's over and it's done. And then you move on."

When Vickery took to the stage in Hull, he says he weighed about 99kg. More defined, but lighter than his playing days when he said his weight would range between 118kg and 135kg.

"[On stage] you look the best version of you that you could look, but you feel the worst. It's kind of a silly sport but it's amazing what the human body can do.

"Age, for me, doesn't bother me at all. I still think I'm 27. My body tells me different."

Training now involves three or four weight sessions a week, combined with daily walks (fasting cardio) and a protein-rich diet.

He hopes more shows will follow in the future.

"I can't do what I used to do and I think the battle for me, certainly when I finished [playing] and even to this day, is you cannot get back those feelings that you had when you used to do what you do," he said.

"I think doing things which can get you outside, test you physically and mentally, and put you in those uncomfortable positions. It's repurposing the skills that you've learned. You've just got to use them in a different way."

Vickery is known for his openness. He posts regularly on his social media channels about his health and fitness. But he's not comfortable with being labelled as an "influencer".

"I don't think everyone should go bodybuilding. My message is trying to be positive. Get out, do something, make a plan."

"I know I will never be a top bodybuilder. But it doesn't stop me, it doesn't stop me having a go and being the best version of me that I can be."

articles.title: Japan v Wales: Flanker Alex Callender to win 50th Welsh cap WXV Test
articles.summary: Wales make three changes to their starting line-up for Saturday's WXV Global Series Test against Japan in Tokyo.
articles.body:
Flanker Alex Callender will win her 50th cap for Wales in Saturday's WXV Global Series game against Japan - while sisters Nel and Branwen Metcalfe will start their first Test together.

Head coach Sean Lynn has made three personnel changes to the starting line-up from September's narrow defeat by USA at Cardiff Arms Park.

Nel Metcalfe returns from injury on the wing, Seren Lockwood is back at scrum-half and Jorja Aiono gets the nod at lock.

There are two positional changes with Carys Cox switching to centre and Keira Bevan starting at fly-half.

Callender, co-captain with fellow back-row forward Kate Williams, will lead Wales out in Tokyo (10:30 BST) when bringing up her half-century of caps.

Live on iplayer and BBC Sport website & app. Audio commentary on Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra & BBC Radio Cymru.

Callender won her first cap in 2019 and hits 50 after returning impressively from injuries suffered before, during and after the 2025 World Cup.

The 26-year-old made a comeback in June's uncapped fixture against the Barbarians, was named as player of the match against South Africa and scored against USA.

"Whenever you talk about a Welsh person everything is about calon and passion - that's her in abundance," said Lynn.

"Whenever she puts that jersey on she wears it with pride and wants to represent the nation. She galvanises this group incredibly, on the pitch and off it."

Callender is a combative flanker but Lynn is quick to point out her deft touches.

"Everybody has always seen Alex as a very passionate individual with phenomenal tackling and breakdown work," said the head coach.

"But she has grown her game and is a really good operator in the line-out and the attack.

"We've been trying to play her as a forward on the edges and she is excelling after working hard on her handling ability over pre-season.

"We're looking to play an expansive game and having a back-row forward who is just like another back brings another dimension."

Quiz: Name the 12 players given Wales debuts by Lynn

Wales use fight for Lions spots as extra incentive

Bevan returns to pulling the strings from fly-half after an encouraging performance alongside Lockwood was ended when the scrum-half suffered a head injury against South Africa.

The score was already 26-5 when the 19-year-old went off, which prompted the introduction of outside half Lleucu George.

"They were super exciting in the first 30 minutes in South Africa game," said Lynn.

"Keira just wants the ball in her hands, she wants to move the ball and her maturity with the kicking game is developing.

"Her performance against USA as a scrum-half was very good as well but we saw the damage that Seren can do against South Africa, and also in the Barbarians fixture when she stood out."

The Metcalfe sisters played for Wales together for the first time when lock Branwen came off the bench for her first cap against Canada at the 2025 World Cup.

They started the uncapped fixture against the Baa-Baas but join forces in the XV for the first time at Test level against Japan.

Branwen, 20, starts her sixth successive Test and has a new second-row partner in fellow bright prospect Aiono.

Nel, 21, returns on the wing rather than full-back for her first cap since the World Cup after a knee injury that forced her to sit out the Six Nations.

"She was a shining light at the World Cup, which was tough for us," said Lynn.

"Every time that she gets the ball, something will happen. She has got fitter, stronger and faster, and she's excited to go out there on Saturday."

Wales are 11th in World Rugby's rankings, a spot above Japan.

Last month the Sakura Fifteen lost 55-21 to Italy and were beaten twice by Ireland, 31-24 in the WXV Global Series and 43-19 in an extra Test.

"Japan ran Ireland close in the first Test and they are very efficient in what they do, very regimented," said Lynn, who opts for six forwards on his bench.

"They've got a very good maul and we are not going to be taking them lightly at all."

articles.title: George Hendy: Northampton Saints back out to fight way into England side
articles.summary: Northampton back George Hendy says he is determined to force his way into England contention, with the autumn internationals looming.
articles.body:
Northampton back George Hendy says he is determined to force his way into England contention, with next month's Nations Championship matches fast approaching.

Hendy has been one of the Saints' form players over the past few seasons, making match-winning contributions in the Prem final victories in 2024 and 2026.

But while a host of club-mates have become regulars for their country, the 24-year-old has had to bide his time.

"I just want to throw my hat in the ring for England and I'm really quite serious about that," Hendy told BBC Sport.

"Whether that's on the wing or at 15, whatever gives me the best opportunity to get into that squad, I want to take it, and I am pretty happy with the direction I am going in."

Northampton 'security incident' believed to be a hoax

Smith set for Quins landmark as Baxter returns

England boss Steve Borthwick will name a training squad on Sunday in preparation for the November leg of the Nations Championship.

Borthwick's side recovered from a chastening Six Nations to win two of their three summer matches, and now welcome Australia, Japan and New Zealand to London before the finals weekend at the end of the month.

A genuine talent with the ball in hand, Hendy says he has been working hard at all parts of his game after conversations with the England management.

"I've known for a while what my work-ons are and it feels like the penny's finally dropping," he added.

"I think my USP is being able to beat defenders and being able to finish tries. And just because I'm working on other things doesn't mean I stop working on that, so I know that if I keep doing that stuff ball in hand whilst touching up the other aspects of my game I'll be in a pretty good spot.

"I've had a few [conversations with the England coaches]. Myself and the Saints coaches know exactly what I need to do to kick on to that next level and all I can do is do that on the weekends."

Hendy says he is inspired by the example of his Northampton team-mates, with Fin Smith, Tommy Freeman, Alex Coles, Alex Mitchell, Henry Pollock and Fraser Dingwall among those to become England stalwarts.

"That makes me want it even more, I think, seeing your mates going and putting on an England shirt and doing what they love doing and representing their country," Hendy said.

"And then you get to see them and you're hearing all about the stories. I just want to be a part of that as well.

"I know that with them in camp, it'll be a good environment. I'll know who I can rely on. I work well with Fin and Tommy Freeman and Mitch.

"All those things, I think, can strengthen my opportunity if I get the chance, so that is what I am going for.

"My motivation is I just don't want to die wondering. I want to at least go into camp and experience it and if I do crack under the pressure of camp then I know that I've still got work to do.

"But it's one of those where you don't know until you get given the opportunity whether you can or you can't.

"So I'm just going to keep putting my best foot forward here and if international call-ups happen they happen and if not, I know I'm not doing a good enough job."

articles.title: South Africa v Ireland: Neve Jones wins 50th Irish cap as Stacey Flood and Dorothy Wall return
articles.summary: Neve Jones wins her 50th Ireland cap as Stacey Flood and Dorothy Wall return for Saturday's WXV Global Series Test against South Africa in Cape Town.
articles.body:
Neve Jones will win her 50th Ireland cap as Stacey Flood and Dorothy Wall return for the first of two WXV Global Series Tests against South Africa in Cape Town.

Gloucester-Hartpury's Jones is named at hooker, while Flood and Wall are reinstalled at full-back and lock for Saturday's game at Athlone Stadium (14:00 BST).

Wall's return to partner Jane Clohessy in the second row means Fione Tuite-O'Sullivan switches to blind-side flanker, while Brittany Hogan starts at number eight to deputise for injured star Aoife Wafer.

Jemima Adams Verling, who filled in for Wafer in the 43-19 win over Japan in Cork on 3 October, drops to the bench.

Flood, who replaces Niamh Gallagher in the 15 jersey, is joined by Beibhinn Parsons and Robyn O'Connor in the back three. Anna McGann and Aoife Dalton are again paired in midfield, while Dannah O'Brien and Emily Lane continue their half-back partnership.

Linda Djougang continues at loose-head prop with Eilis Cahill at tight-head either side of Jones, while Erin King captains the team from open-side flanker.

Kate Jordan, who made her debut as a second-half replacement for King in the win over Japan, is one of six forwards on the bench alongside Beth Buttimer, Niamh O'Dowd, Sadhbh McGrath, Grace Moore and Adams Verling.

Aoibheann Reilly and Eve Higgins provide backline cover from the bench.

Ireland's only previous meeting with South Africa was a 2006 Women's Rugby World Cup match in Canada, which the Irish won 37-0.

Scott Bemand's side opened their WXV campaign with defeat by the United States before bouncing back to beat Japan in Galway. They also defeated Japan in Cork in a non-WXV Test match in Cork.

After Saturday's first meeting, Ireland face South Africa again in Cape Town on 31 October.

articles.title: French teenage rugby player dies after on-field injury
articles.summary: A 17-year-old amateur rugby player dies after suffering an on-field injury during a match for Union du Bassin Marmandais.
articles.body:
A 17-year-old amateur rugby player has died after suffering an on-field injury during a match in France.

Clea Menier - a back row for Union du Bassin Marmandais - died after what her club said was an "accident" during an under-18s match against Agen Agglo Rugby on Saturday.

After receiving medical attention on the field, the teenager was taken to Pellegrin Hospital in Bordeaux, where she died from her injuries.

Neither the club nor the French Rugby Federation (FFR) have disclosed the nature of her injury.

"It is with immense sadness and indescribable pain that Union du Bassin Marmandais learned of the death of Clea," the club said in a statement, which paid tribute to the emergency services who treated her.

"We are also thinking of her loved ones and friends, whose immense pain we share, as well as her team-mates, coaches, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing her and sharing their passion for rugby with her.

"This is a terrible ordeal for our club. We will get through it together - united, standing in solidarity, and looking after one another."

The FFR said: "This loss has deeply shaken the entire rugby family.

"In these moments of sadness, the FFR wishes to express its full support and solidarity to Clea's family and loved ones.

"It also extends its sincerest condolences to her team-mates, coaches, and all members of Union du Bassin Marmandais.

"Every effort will be made to understand the circumstances surrounding this accident."

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: England travel schedule like Planes, Trains and Automobiles - McDermott
articles.summary: England were left exhausted before the start of their Rugby League World Cup campaign because of a travel schedule straight out of Planes, Trains and Automobiles, head coach Brian McDermott says.
articles.body:
England were left exhausted and with little preparation time for the start of their Rugby League World Cup campaign because of a travel schedule straight out of the film Planes, Trains and Automobiles, head coach Brian McDermott says.

England's 30-12 defeat by Tonga last Saturday has left them teetering on the brink of elimination because of the unusual format of this year's tournament.

However, the UK-based players in McDermott's squad were hardly helped by a lengthy trip to their Perth base, taking almost 48 hours.

Speaking to the media on Thursday, McDermott likened it to the hapless journey undertaken by Steve Martin and John Candy in their 1987 road-trip comedy.

"We were going around the world 15 times to arrive in Perth. We were [exhausted] for about three days afterwards," said McDermott.

"I think we were on the same aeroplane as John Candy and Steve Martin, for all you who remember Planes, Trains and Automobiles.

"I had to call Monday's training session short because you could tell there was a load of residue from travel still left in them."

BBC Sport understands that the International Rugby League - the game's global governing body and the tournament organiser - planned England's travel itinerary for the World Cup. The BBC has contacted the IRL for comment.

Rugby League World Cup: England v France

Listen to live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

The convoluted route featured players taking a bus journey from the north of England to London before flying to Singapore instead of directly to Perth.

Instead of taking a five-hour flight from Singapore to Perth, England then flew for almost eight hours to Sydney, before catching another plane to go back to Western Australia.

It meant the McDermott's new-look side completed just two full training sessions before taking on a powerful Tonga side, two places below them in fifth in the IRL world rankings.

And despite showing promise, there were also elements to England's play that understandably fell short - given there was no time to schedule a warm-up match for a team who have not played since losing the third Ashes Test to Australia at Headingley in November 2025 under Shaun Wane, McDermott's predecessor.

"I think we did really well, and if you give me another two or three weeks preparation or another couple of games of preparation leading into the tournament, I'd be really excited," added McDermott, who took charge in April following Wane's departure.

England's 'slim chance' to advance down to format

The result means, in order to reach the semi-finals, England will have to defeat France on Saturday (07:35 BST) and Papua New Guinea on Friday, 30 October (09:05 GMT) and also see other results go in their favour.

Their task has been made all the more difficult by Samoa's thumping 78-4 win over France, which means England's points difference is 92 worse than that of Ben Gardiner's team in a combined Pool B and C table.

The format features an unbalanced group stage, which has not helped England's prospects.

Pool A has four teams - Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands - fighting for two semi-final places in a round-robin format.

But Pools B and C are combined into one six-team league, from which only the top two will make the semi-finals. England, drawn in Pool B, are playing the three Pool C teams - Tonga, France and Papua New Guinea.

It means that while England are in deep trouble after one defeat, New Zealand still have a strong chance of making the last four despite losing to favourites Australia in a high-quality opening match.

"The jeopardy of losing one game is so harsh, it's almost like we don't get another chance to straighten things out," added McDermott.

"There's still a slim chance that we get through, and that's something we're focusing on and we're really determined.

"New Zealand have lost their first game as well, but they're going to get another go at it and the likelihood is they'll qualify, so their destiny is not lying in other people's hands. That's not the position we find ourselves in."

McDermott has named an unchanged 19-man squad for the game against France but has confirmed that Warrington's Matty Ashton will start in place of Wigan's Zach Eckersley on the wing.

The England head coach made clear he did not want to criticise either the hosts or the organisers for the tournament's unusual format.

Instead, he pointed out that it resulted from Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea having to step in at short notice after France pulled out of hosting the tournament for financial reasons.

He added: "I'm trying to be diplomatic here. If France had held the World Cup, there would have been more teams in it. It would have had the usual pools for the teams.

"You've got to give Australia a lot of credit for taking it on the last minute.

"But because they [France] haven't, I completely understand that it has to be reduced to a 10-team competition, which is not the easiest thing to do and then we end up in situations like this."

articles.title: England: Red Roses out for revenge after Canada end four-year unbeaten run - but is that good for women's rugby?
articles.summary: Canada’s women snapped world champion England’s 41-match unbeaten run with a 24-21 victory in Toronto last Friday; last month, Canada also drew with England 26-26 in Exeter to halt the Red Roses' 39-Test winning run; Canada host England in Ottawa this Friday, October 23
articles.body:
Between their galling 2022 Women's Rugby World Cup final defeat to New Zealand at Eden Park and last week, the Red Roses went 41 Tests unbeaten, winning 39 consecutive matches before a draw against Canada in Exeter last month.

England's dominance is even more stark when you take into account that before that 2022 defeat, they had gone on a 30-Test winning run between November 2019 and November 2022.

Before last week in Canada, therefore, England had won 70 of their previous 72 Test matches. Astonishing and remarkable in equal measure.

Some eight Six Nations titles have been won in a row, in near totally dominant fashion too between 2019 and 2026, while a third World Cup triumph to sit alongside 1994 and 2014 was finally clinched on home soil in 2025, after final defeats in 2017 and 2022.

And yet, such monumentally impressive dominance had placed England in a position where Six Nations contests were fast becoming a non-event, competition-wise.

While France and New Zealand had historically competed hard and alongside England at the top of the world game, and Ireland won Six Nations titles in 2013 and 2015, the Red Roses were now consistently blowing those sides away completely.

Canada's rise in recent years can only be a good thing for the sport, as is the apparent resurgence of New Zealand's Black Ferns. They were level with England at 19-19 at Twickenham last month and pushing for a late winner in the final play, only for the Red Roses to snatch victory themselves .

In 2023, England put 50 points and 45 points on Canada in one-sided Test wins. By the 2025 World Cup final at Twickenham, Canada were competitive until England proved too strong and pulled away to glory.

But a year on, Canada have drawn with England in Exeter and now fought back to beat them in Toronto from a position of 21-12 behind. Friday's third Test between the sides in Ottawa is now a genuinely compelling and tantalising prospect. That can only be seen as a good thing for women's rugby.

Mitchell: Defeat is 'definitely' what Red Roses needed

Red Roses head coach John Mitchell has borderline talked up a defeat for his side in recent months.

Indeed, it appears the 62-year-old anticipated this WXV Global Series block was going to prove testing for his side, and is now relishing the chance to hit back.

"Definitely [it is what England needed]," he said. "I think even before that message we said: 'Come and get us.'

"We have been asking for someone to come and get us and they have done that. Not that we designed that to happen, far from it. We have to respond.

"The important thing is winning after winning is harder than before. I guess what it does to everyone is it frees us up, which is cool. It allows us all to find more.

"I know this group has definitely got more in it but sometimes it requires the context that we have just received to dig deeper and push for something more.

"Friday is our first chance to respond. Last Friday, we lost sight of what we could control when it mattered most and that's on us to fix.

"This week is about getting back to who we are: hungry, accountable to each other and demanding more of ourselves than anyone outside this group ever could.

"We've earned a strong period, but nothing about it is owed to us going forward. Friday is an opportunity to apply sustained pressure, learn from what we missed and come out the other side better than we went in."

Jones: I know this will make Red Roses stronger

Red Roses centre Meg Jones has proven an inspirational leader since taking on the captaincy earlier this year, and was so even before the official title came her way.

In this period of pressure and spotlight, so unusual for the Red Roses, her soundbites to media have nearly all been pitch perfect.

"For us the biggest thing is that we stick together," she said this week.

"Games are built on moments, it is not one individual moment, it is multiple. That is the beauty of it and we get to review it, we get to go again, we get to stick together.

"I think it is good for us to reassess this and see where we are at. I think togetherness is the main message to come out of that because it's how you respond when you have had a loss, I think that is the biggest test of character.

"They are lessons at the end of the day, I don't think a loss necessarily changes the way we approach things. You genuinely do learn from it.

"I spoke to Burts [Abi Burton] and we said: 'How many games have we lost in our career?' And we had a little chuckle, those are the ones that shape you the most at times. It's the biggest lesson for sure. Teams are coming out to beat us, they are going to put their best foot forward. We need to make sure we have got our best foot forward as well.

"It tests our game a lot, and it shows our character. We've just gained massive amounts of experience, and I know it'll make us stronger going into each game.

"Now we have the opportunity to not be defined by the outcome and really solidify where your two feet are and where you are is the most important. That is where you find courage and bravery to stick where you are in the present moment. That is going to be huge for us this weekend."

'Everything we do this year is to beat England'

And what of Canada? A year ago, they crowdfunded their way to a World Cup final against England at Twickenham, producing one of the tournament's standout performances along the way by beating New Zealand 34-19 at Ashton Gate with a swashbuckling brand of rugby.

Bringing together players from eight of Canada's 13 vast provinces and territories, spread across six time zones, and giving them the best possible preparation for the World Cup prompted a fundraising campaign with a target of C$1m (£535,355). Rugby Canada made its ambitions clear, dubbing it Mission: Win Rugby World Cup 2025.

Pledges reached 95 per cent of the target, helping fund training camps in California, Ontario and Belfast, as well as warm-up Tests in South Africa and Ireland.

Since rugby turned openly professional in 1995, Canada's women's sevens and 15s teams have become the country's flagship sides, surpassing the men's team. But Rugby Canada has lacked the resources to fully contract them.

As a result, world No 2 Canada are not a fully professional outfit like top-ranked England, but the gap between the two sides feels narrower than ever.

In September, Canada scrum-half Olivia Apps told the media that "everything we do this year is to beat England". True to their word, the Canadians have now done just that.

"When you've done it once, you want to do it twice," Canada head coach Kevin Rouet said this week.

"But to do it twice, you have to be serious. We have to enjoy, but we have to go back to the grind."

Also this week, Rouet signed a new contract with Canada through to 2030 as they build towards the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles and at Women's Rugby World Cup 2029.

"I am very excited for the opportunity to continue coaching this team for the next four years. We have grown so much as a group since I began in 2022, and I am excited to see what our teams and players can achieve as we build towards the 2028 Olympics and the 2029 Rugby World Cup.

"I also look forward to continuing to help develop the high-performance pathway for women's rugby in Canada. It's going to be an exciting next cycle."

articles.title: WRU says £18m loss shows why regional team must be axed
articles.summary: The Welsh Rugby Union blames rising energy and staffing costs combined with falling ticket sales for a dramatic drop in its finances.
articles.body:
The Welsh Rugby Union has spelled out the "tough" economic state of the game in Wales - despite suggesting its financial position was "pretty good" just five months ago.

The governing body has announced a significant decline in its finances, saying it has posted an £18m loss for the financial year to June 2026 - compared to a £7.2m loss the previous year.

Financial boss Gavin Marshall admitted the figures were disappointing and came despite turnover rising £10m to £116.2m.

Just five months ago, new chief financial and operating officer Marshall claimed the WRU's finances were in a "pretty good position".

But it says that rising energy and staffing costs, combined with falling ticket sales and reduced fan spend, were to blame for the dramatic fall.

The union says it is already predicting a similar loss next year, and said the figures back up its case that four professional regions are no longer sustainable.

"We can't go on like this," said Marshall.

The financial performance of the WRU, on the back of the controversial decision to cut the number of regions from four to three , is sure to provoke dismay, frustration and even anger from clubs and fans.

"The numbers are tough and not where we want them to be, but it's been a challenging year," said Marshall.

"As an executive team we are accountable for these numbers, so we have to look at our performance and where we can do better.

"But we can only control certain things and it's a tough world out there impacting all sport with the cost of living crisis affecting what people spend as well as our own costs.

"We should be aiming to break even but we're quite some way off where we want to be. I'm ambitious and we need to grow our way out of that deficit but the gap, right now, is stark."

WRU publishes data on why west Wales team will be cut

What Welsh shake-up means and why it matters to rest of rugby world

Can people fall back in love with Welsh rugby?

The WRU insists Welsh rugby is "living beyond its means" and cannot go on sustaining such losses.

The official accounts for the past financial year are expected to be lodged with Companies House on Friday but have already been shared with clubs.

The WRU's audited annual report for the 2023 financial year showed new profit and loss figures for the previous two years, with the loss in 2023 re-listed as £14m up from £4.9m - although the profit in 2022 now stood at £37.3m rather than £2.9m.

Since that re-audited positive 2022 figure, the financial situation has continued to decline.

When former WRU chair Richard Collier-Keywood and a new board took charge at the start of 2024, he admitted the finances were "a mess".

In an interview with the BBC the following year he revealed the extent of the problem, saying that "in January 2024 the WRU had run out of money - we were up against our overdraft limit".

The WRU had taken out an £18m Covid support loan from the Welsh government in 2022, for which it subsequently appealed for an improvement in terms.

But a new £55m debt-refinancing package agreed in January 2026 - via banks HSBC and Goldman Sachs - was designed to see the Welsh government loan and a separate commercial loan paid off.

In the past few years, the union has also paid out £1.9m to departing employees, as well as keeping Cardiff afloat since taking over the struggling region in April 2025.

The WRU will struggle to avoid the accusation from west Wales that the regions threatened with closure - Ospreys and Scarlets, who have been approached for comment - are paying the price for the WRU's financial performance.

"We have a lot of costs, including the stadium [£26m], the national teams [£20m], interest on our loan [£3m], funding community rugby [£4m]," said Marshall.

"That leaves about £20m to invest in professional rugby but at the moment we're funding £26m across the four clubs. From a financial perspective, we just can't afford that.

"We need to grow revenue but also sensibly manage our costs, investments and distribution of funds.

"We could have as many clubs as you want but it's how you fund those clubs, how competitive they can be with that funding and how much benefactor funding goes into the clubs. At the moment we're not sustainable."

The men's national team is the biggest driving factor behind the WRU's revenue, contributing almost half its income.

So it is clear that while a successful Wales boosts the coffers, a team on a record losing run, as Steve Tandy's side were until March, sees income stall.

Empty seats for last year's home Test against world champions South Africa and again in the Six Nations game against France reflected a declining appetite among fans who, on average, are also spending less when they do attend the Principality Stadium.

"We hosted seven men's internationals compared with five the previous year but match income increased by only £2m," said Marshall.

"This was challenging and reflected lower average ticket prices, some lower attendances and the global economic pressure on consumer spending."

The WRU is now caught between encouraging more fans to buy tickets - broadening the price categories from three to six - and the need to maximise income from those key matches.

Adding fuel to the fire from west Wales is the WRU sustaining Cardiff's £1.2m loss for the past financial year.

That figure is not startling given Ospreys and Scarlets both lost more the previous year - the most recent figures on record.

The union took over the failing region in April 2025 and while a deal with Ospreys owners Y11 Sport & Media later fell through , Marshall confirmed Cardiff will be put up for sale again, though not until the current shake-up is complete.

That could mean holding on to Cardiff until at least 2028.

"The strategy is not to own Cardiff but we decided that while we are in this restructure and level of uncertainty, it's a tough environment to sell a club," he said.

"When there's certainty for Welsh rugby, that will enable us to find the right buyer and right value for the Cardiff."

The WRU aims to increase the number and range of non-rugby events at the Principality Stadium.

While concerts only raise modest funds, they are seen as risk-free opportunities given promoters pay rent for the venue while the WRU earns from food and drink sales.

However, they face rising costs and increasing competition from other venues, which will include a new 16,500 music arena under construction in Cardiff Bay, while Kanye West - set for two nights at the stadium - was refused entry to the UK.

But football's Community Shield returned to Cardiff in August while the stadium will host world heavyweight boxing between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua in December, before summer concerts by Andrea Bocelli and Sam Fender.

However, Marshall confirmed there are no immediate plans for the regional derby event Judgement Day to return to the stadium.

These latest figures will come under scrutiny from member clubs at next month's annual general meeting (AGM).

Marshall also confirmed the WRU had received £9.6m for its stake in a portion of United Rugby Championship (URC) shares - shared by all five competing unions - sold to private equity firm CVC Capital Partners.

The one-off deal will mean less participation money each year from the league but the WRU insisted Cardiff, Dragons, Ospreys and Scarlets will get enough of the £9.6m to cover that reduction.

Meanwhile, the union remains committed to its investment in the community game and pointed to a profit made by the Parkgate Hotel it owns in Cardiff.

However, the WRU has already raised worrying concerns for the next financial year as it is already predicting an operating loss of £16m.

"Our responsibility is to build a financially stronger organisation capable of supporting the game at every level," added Marshall.
